transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Evan Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kumar (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Redwood CSM), Jamal Peterson (Acme CTO), Lena Ortiz (Acme SRE), Marco Rivera (Acme PM)

Summary (auto): Short follow-up to the 2026-02-18 production incident affecting checkout tokenization; confirm mitigations, share postmortem artifacts, agree long-term reliability changes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on short notice. we wanted to go through the postmortem and next steps, make sure there's clarity on root cause, and agree on mitigations.
[00:10] Jamal: Yep thanks, appreciate the follow-up. we had a pretty bad spike friday, transactions queued and latency went into the red, so we're anxious to understand why the fallback to the dedicated pool didn't happen.
[00:22] Priya: Right. quick recap from our side — initial triage points to an autoscaler race that caused ephemeral workers to not be provisioned fast enough and a cascade of KV cache cold misses which drove tokenization latency. that combined with the routing policy favoring hosted instances under certain health checks; so slightly multi-factor.
[00:45] Lena: Can you unpack the KV cache bit? our telemetry shows a big drop in cache hit rate around 14:12 UTC.
[00:52] Priya: yes, so when the new requests for longer sequences hit, the KV cache had been evicted during the GC window and the first round of requests had to rebuild large prefixes. there's also an off-by-one in the autoscaler cooldown config that prevented warm nodes from spinning up in time — it's basically a timing/threshold mismatch.
[01:15] Marco: Is that a Redwood config or something we set on the Dedicated side? we thought the dedicated pool was pinned.
[01:23] Evan: good question. the dedicated pool is pinned but we had a burst policy that allows shared-hosted to route while the dedicated pool is ramping; the combination exposed the cooldown issue. so partially our config suggestion plus the burst routing policy.
[01:40] Jamal: that routing bit is new to us — we were under the impression traffic is always on dedicated for critical endpoints.
[01:46] Maya: we should've clarified that in the runbook, sorry about that. the default recommendation sometimes includes short burst to hosted to avoid hard failures, but for strict SLO customers we recommend disabling burst; we didn't have that onboarding locked for this route.
[02:05] Lena: Ok — so practically what stopped traffic from shifting immediately to dedicated?
[02:12] Priya: autoscaler cooldown of 120s combined with a threshold set to 50% CPU; the traffic spike pushed request concurrency but nodes were not yet marked as healthy because of a liveness probe timing, so the routing continued to fan out. we patched the healthcheck timing during the incident and that restored routing, but the KV cache rebuild cost remained high for several minutes.
[02:36] Jamal: Are the patches you're referring to permanent? we need a durable fix not just the incident patch.
[02:41] Evan: what we deployed on Friday were short term mitigations: 1) temporarily lowered autoscaler cooldown to 30s, 2) increased the readiness probe timeout to avoid premature health flapping, 3) pre-warmed a small set of instances with your 95th percentile prompt set. those are live now.
[03:03] Marco: Pre-warming helped — but we saw variable improvements across regions.
[03:08] Priya: yeah region variance is expected due to different cold-start baselines and variations in traffic shape.
[03:15] Lena: on the logs you sent there were a few s3 timeouts noted — are those related?
[03:20] Priya: we did see some retries to object storage for certain model artifacts; those added a few 100s of ms in the worst path but weren't the primary root cause. we'll include the sanitized logs in the postmortem.
[03:36] Jamal: Ok. i'd like to understand the customer-facing impact: how many requests were erroring vs just slow?
[03:43] Maya: from our combined telemetry roughly 0.8% failures (5xx) during the 8-minute window, and latencies spiked for ~7 minutes — the checkout flow retries amplified user-visible failures.
[04:00] Marco: that matches our observability, we used backoff but some sessions timed out at the UI.
[04:07] Evan: Action-wise — we think three tracks: immediate config hardening (disable burst routing for critical routes, adjust autoscaler thresholds), monitoring and alerting improvements (KV cache hit-rate alerting, early warning on readiness probe flapping), and runbook + chaos testing to ensure this sequence doesn't recur.
[04:25] Lena: sounds good. for monitoring, can you add a dashboard we can access with the hit-rate and a short description of the alert thresholds?
[04:32] Priya: yes we'll share a dashboard link and a recommended alert rule.
[04:36] Jamal: Also we need the security sanitized logs — SOC 2 folks will want those for the postmortem.
[04:43] Evan: we'll provide them, sanitized and filtered for PII, and include the KMS key IDs used.
[04:49] Marco: timeline question — when will the full postmortem land?
[04:53] Maya: we committed to 48 hours; evan?
[04:56] Evan: yes we'll send a doc by 2026-02-22 with timeline, root cause analysis, metric graphs, and remediation plan.
[05:02] Marco: ok thanks.
[05:06] Lena: i'd like to request a small change to the autoscaler: lower cooldown and different health probe semantics for your dedicated pool only. is that possible?
[05:14] Priya: yes we can make pool-specific autoscaler profiles. the change itself is quick but we'll need to validate in staging for 24h and then can push to prod.
[05:24] Jamal: any concerns about stability if cooldown is lowered?
[05:28] Priya: risk is flapping/oscillation — we mitigate that by making step-scaling more conservative and adding a short warm-up window. we'll document the parameters.
[05:38] Evan: one other improvement: adding prefix/KV cache checkpointing for very hot prefixes to reduce rebuild cost; this is more of an engineering change but high-impact.
[05:48] Marco: timeline on that?
[05:50] Priya: rough estimate is 2-3 sprints to design & test, but we can scope a smaller incremental which pins the hot-prefixes for 24h — that could be faster.
[06:02] Jamal: are there any recommended config toggles we should set immediately?
[06:06] Evan: immediate: disable burst routing for checkout route, set autoscaler cooldown to 30s for your dedicated pool, enable our pre-warm hook with your 95p prompt set; medium: add KV cache hit-rate alerts and a dashboard; long: checkpointing and improved kernel fallbacks.
[06:23] Marco: ok, can you include exact CLI or console steps in the doc? we want to hand to infra to apply if agreed.
[06:29] Priya: will do, the doc will have the console screenshots and terraform snippet.
[06:34] Lena: about audits — will the postmortem include a changelog of what was changed in prod? we need that for our audit trail.
[06:41] Maya: yes we'll include a full changelog and the release IDs.
[06:45] Jamal: i want to raise a related item: incident communications. we noticed status page had lag. can Redwood help with faster status updates or templates?
[06:55] Evan: absolutely, we can share a notification template and coordinate a runbook that includes pre-written messages.
[07:03] Marco: one more item — can you run a production-like test with our traffic shape next week? we can provide a capture of top 1% sessions.
[07:11] Priya: yes we can schedule a bench run; we'll need the payload capture and a window from you.
[07:16] Lena: sending that today.
[07:18] Evan: great. to recap next steps: evan will send postmortem by 2/22, priya will share dashboards and bench plan, maya will schedule runbook, acme will share traffic capture and timeline. any other open asks?
[07:33] Jamal: please include the sanitized logs with KMS info and the list of user-facing error codes.
[07:38] Evan: yes.
[07:40] Marco: let's meet again after the runbook tabletop; target week of 3/2.
[07:45] Maya: i'll send invites.
[07:47] Evan: thanks all, we'll follow up in the doc.
[07:50] Lena: thanks everyone.
[07:52] Meeting end.
